newsitem.title: Indonesia: Indonesia's Golkar head for landslide poll win.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Golkar head for landslide poll win.

text.p: Indonesia's ruling Golkar, assured of a general election victory even before voting began, headed for a landslide win on Friday after a campaign hit by the worst political violence in three decades.
The country was generally calm, although angry Moslems protesting the size of the Golkar win on Madura island, burned a housing complex, offices and a church after the polls on Thursday.
In the former Portuguese colony of East Timor, where at least 17 people have died in poll-related violence, police chief Colonel Yusuf Muharam said the situation was "calm and under control".
Golkar had won more than 73 percent of 96 million votes counted out of a potential 125 million by 10:30 a.m. (0330 GMT).
Its main opponent, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PDI), was making a good showing with nearly 24 percent, while the badly split Indonesian Democratric Party (PDI) had 2.86 percent.

Political and financial analysts had expressed concerns over possible violence, particularly in Jakarta, if PPP supporters felt they had been cheated in the vote. But the only reported PPP trouble was on Madura, off Java's east coast, and police there said it was calm again on Friday morning.

Analysts said Golkar's showing was generally within expectations after the party had sought just over 70 percent of the vote compared to the 68 percent it won in the last elections in 1992. Its best showing had been 73.17 percent in 1987.
"The results are not surprising," one diplomatic analyst said, adding that there had also been protests over the Golkar vote in previous elections and this was to be expected.

"However, nobody expected the PDI to collapse like this," one foreign observer said. The PDI was virtually sidelined during the 27-day campaign by a bitter leadership battle after Megawati Sukarnoputri, eldest daughter of late founding president Sukarno, was ousted as party chief last year by a government-backed rival, Surjadi.
Analysts said Golkar would benefit from spoiled ballots or abstentions, particularly by disaffected PDI members.
But a senior Asian diplomat said he did not expect the so-called Golput (White Party) vote -- spoiled ballots and abstentions -- to be much above the three-to-four percent that occurred in 1992.
Analysts said President Suharto could be well satisfied with Golkar's vote, which would ease his way to an expected seventh five-year term in March next year.
The Asian diplomat, however, said Thursday's elections should not be seen as a vote on Suharto himself. It will not affect the makeup of the cabinet or government policy.
"The election is not a mandate for Suharto, it's not a judgement on him, but it does make it easier for Suharto to be re-elected," he said.
Analysts generally see the presidential poll next year as the key election for the country, with keen interest in who the 75-year-old president will select as a running mate and potential successor.

Analyst Dewi Fortuna Anwar of the Centre for Information and Development Studies said she considered Thursday's vote generally free. The two minority parties had objected to the way the system was stacked against them in favour of Golkar, she added.
"In terms of the election itself, I think it's free, so it is not the election itself that is the problem. If Golkar wins, I don't think it will be bacause of vote manipulation or anything like that.
"It's just that conditions are made which mean it is quite hard for Golkar to lose," she said.
